title: Panel Examines the Ascencio Rosario v. Mexico Judgment and Its Human Rights Implications - Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center
content: In December 2025, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued its judgment in Ascencio Rosario et al. v. Mexico, a case co-litigated by Kennedy Human Rights Center after nearly two decades of seeking justice for Ernestina Ascencio Rosario and her family. On September 2, 2026, our International Advocacy & Litigation team joined a discussion hosted by the Casas de los Saberes Jurídicos of Mexico’s Supreme Court to reflect on the judgment’s significance and the opportunities it creates to strengthen human rights protections in Mexico. Alongside our co-counsel Carmen Herrera and representatives from Mexican judicial and human rights institutions, KHRC Wilson Fellow Paulina Macías discussed key standards developed by the Inter-American Court in this landmark decision, including those related to sexual violence, intersectional discrimination, and the particular barriers Indigenous women face in accessing health care and justice. The discussion also explored how these standards should inform the work of Mexican judicial and public authorities beyond the individual case. Panelists reflected on the need to confront institutional responses rooted in denial, discrimination, and stereotyping; strengthen Indigenous women’s access to truth, health care, and justice; ensure meaningful reparations for victims and their families; and translate the Court’s guarantees of non-repetition into lasting institutional change. title: Liverpool v Tottenham player ratings from Carabao Cup as youngsters shine but Spurs stars flop - Yahoo Sports
content: A much-changed Liverpool side knocked Tottenham out of the Carabao Cup to continue their winless start to the season under Roberto De Zerbi. Spurs named a strong team, started well and should have taken a first-half lead when a cross fell to the feet of Lucas Bergvall in the box, but goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili made a stunning stop to deny him. Liverpool then almost cut through Spurs as Rio Ngumoha found Lewis Koumas, only to be denied by Martin Dubravka, before Alexis Mac Allister fired the opening goal with a first-time shot into the top corner from the edge of the box. Tottenham had not come from behind to win in 47 previous attempts and their task became even harder when Cody Gakpo cut inside from the left and slammed Liverpool into a two-goal lead shortly after the break. Conor Gallagher belatedly scored Tottenham's first goal of the season to set up a frantic ending, but Dominik Szoboszlai's late rocket sent Liverpool through to the fourth round. Giorgi Mamardashvili, 8: Liverpool's No 2 goalkeeper made an excellent early stop to deny Lucas Bergvall when the tie was goalless, and another from Omar Marmoush later on. But he looked weak from the corner that led to Tottenham's goal. Jeremie Frimpong, 5: Both of Tottenham's big first-half chances came down his side while, in an attacking sense, his final ball from the right was poor once again. But stuck to his task against the lively Mathys Tel. Ronald Araujo, 7: The only player to keep his place from Saturday's 0-0 draw with Fulham. He displayed authority in the backline in another promising display from the on-loan Barcelona centre-back. Joe Gomez, 6: Perhaps some rust would have been expected as the injury-prone defender made his first start of the season, but he slotted in well enough in a 45-minute showing and had a role in Mac Allister's goal. Milos Kerkez, 6: Solid enough defensively, with some bright bursts going forward too. An excellent recovery challenge to deny Omar Marmoush in the box was his highlight. Alexis Mac Allister, 8: Delivered another big Anfield goal on a night where Liverpool needed his experience and he showed up. Showed his class at times. Trey Nyoni, 7: Deployed in the deep-lying midfield position, the 19-year-old didn't put a foot wrong once he had adjusted to the pace of the game and Tottenham's fast start. Rio Ngumoha, 7: Produced a wonderful turn and pass to set up an early chance for Lewis Koumas and also had a hand in Mac Allister's opener. The 18-year-old continues to adjust to the right side of attack. James McConnell, 7: A very bright showing, full of energy, and led the hugely improved Liverpool press that rather set the tone for the night. Like Nyoni, didn't look out of place. Cody Gakpo, 8: Continued his superb start to the season with a trademark finish while coming inside onto his right foot. Brought incision to Liverpool's attack and scored while wearing the armband, too. Lewis Koumas, 7: Didn't stop running all night and worked his socks off, despite playing in an unfamiliar position. Had an excellent chance to open the scoring after making a peeling run but was denied by Dubravka. Jeremy Jacquet, 7: Made an excellent recovery challenge on Marmoush in the second half. Ryan Gravenberch, 6: Liverpool actually lost some control after he replaced Nyoni. Dominik Szoboszlai, 7: Wowzer. What a way to seal victory - and after wasting a late chance to put the game to bed. Bradley Barcola, N/A: Showed some electric pace on the counter-attack, but Frimpong couldn't find him. Alexander Isak, N/A: Led a very late breakaway but could not find the target. Martin Dubravka, 6: Made a good save to deny Koumas early on but was well beaten on the three Liverpool goals. Archie Gray, 5: One of Tottenham's better performers in the first half but allowed Gakpo onto his right foot far too easily. Tosin Adarabioyo, 5: Looks to be Tottenham's fourth-choice centre-back and hardly suggested he deserves to be any higher. Marcos Senesi, 4: Caught out on the ball on a couple of occasions when playing out from the back. Destiny Udogie, 5: Showed up well in his battle with Ngumoha and offered a couple of moments from threat from left back. Rodrigo Bentancur, 4: Looked slow on the ball and off the pace. Blitzed by Liverpool's young midfielders at times. Spurs struggled against Liverpool's midfield shape (Getty) Lucas Bergvall, 6: Produced a couple of bursts forward but spurned a brilliant chance to open the scoring. Mohammed Kudus, 6: Wasted a glorious chance to equalise from under the crossbar but brought some flashes on his first start of the season. Conor Gallagher, 4: Scored Tottenham's first goal of the season, at long last, but he was wasteful on the ball at times and guilty of some loose touches in midfield. Mathys Tel, 5: Crafted a couple of opportunities for others on the left wing, but brought off in the second half without having made enough impact. Omar Marmoush, 6: Similarly, had bright moments. Struggled leading the line but then was denied by an excellent Mamardashvili after fashioning a chance for himself coming off the left. Andy Robertsons, 6: Came on to an excellent reception on his Anfield return. Matheus Fernandes, 7: Tottenham improved when he was added to the midfield. John Stegeman launched a fierce attack in front of the ESPN cameras after Ajax v Willem II (5-1) over a striking new rule. Because of that rule, Jaden Slory had to spend a minute on the sidelines after being hit in the face by Steven Berghuis. "Ridiculous," said Stegeman. Late in the first half, Berghuis and Slory both went for the ball deep inside Ajax's half, with Berghuis catching the Willem II forward in the face with his arm. Slory stayed down on the turf for a long time before Lindhout decided to stop play. "Yes, that was not a collision. He hits him in the face. Allard Lindhout also admitted just now that it was a foul," said Stegeman, who is not even frustrated about Berghuis not being shown a card. Lindhout's decision to stop play still meant Slory had to wait on the sidelines for a minute, and that is what really infuriates Stegeman. "Jaden gets something in his face, the referee blows the whistle, and then he has to go off for a minute. That is something I can get angry about. Well, whoever that idiot was who came up with it... The KNVB can't do anything about it as far as I'm concerned, because they have to apply the rules. But it really is ridiculous." "I don't know what kind of people are sitting there (at IFAB, ed.), but in my view they have nothing to do with football," Stegeman continued to rage. "I think it's a very unusual rule. I understand it for time-wasting, but he just gets a hand in his face. Fine, if the whistle doesn't go, and maybe it was yellow or red, but that's not the point." "But in this situation, if you then have to go off for a minute, we are simply playing a minute a man down against Ajax. Yes, that really can get on my nerves, I have to say. Yes, I even got booked for it, nice one. I was furious. But I think all my colleagues feel the same, it's just a very strange rule." "Every year they come up with a few new rules again, and there really are some good ones among them. With regard to time-wasting, fine. But in the end this one really makes no sense at all. If there is something the KNVB can do about it, then do it very quickly." Stegeman insisted the incident had little bearing on the result. "Ajax simply played a very good match. title: John V. Marano - The New Era | Sweet Home, OR
content: John V. Marano, 79, of Sweet Home, passed away on Tuesday, Sept.1, 2026. He was born on May 11,1947 to Flornell May (Weiman) and Samuel Vincent Marano in Johnstown, Pa. John lived a life centered around the things that mattered most to him: his faith, his family, and the outdoors. John’s love for the Lord Jesus Christ was a meaningful part of his life and something he carried with him throughout his years. Family was also deeply important to John, and he treasured the many relationships, memories, and moments shared with those he loved. John was happiest outdoors, particularly when he was hunting or simply enjoying the beauty and peacefulness of nature. He also loved his beloved dogs, who were more than pets to him. They were faithful companions and an important part of his family. John is survived by his beloved wife, Barbara Marano; his children, Matthew (Jessica) Marano and Tori (Joe) Brown; his stepchildren, Catharyn (Mark) Crawford, Truman (Sheila) Jones and John Jones; and his many cherished grandchildren. John will be remembered for the love he had for his family, his faith in the Lord, and the things that brought him joy throughout his life. His absence will be deeply felt, but those who loved him find comfort in knowing he is now home with the Lord. A memorial service will be held at noon Saturday, Sept. 26, at Full Gospel Church, 2331 Highway 20, Sweet Home. Sweet Home Funeral Chapel is handling the arrangements.

title: Saw V, Saw VI and Saw VII Coming to 4K UHD in November 2026 - Seat42F
content: Home - Movies - Saw V, Saw VI and Saw VII Coming to 4K UHD in November 2026 Jigsaw’s legacy is getting a major 4K upgrade. Lionsgate is bringing Saw V, Saw VI and Saw VII, also known as Saw: The Final Chapter, to 4K UHD, Blu-ray and Digital on November 10, 2026. The three releases continue the horror franchise’s Detective Hoffman era, with Costas Mandylor taking center stage alongside Tobin Bell’s John Kramer. Each release includes both the theatrical and extended or unrated version of the film, legacy bonus material and newly produced Blu-ray features created specifically for the 2026 editions. Saw V, Saw VI and Saw VII will be available to preorder beginning September 29. Lionsgate will release Saw V, Saw VI and Saw VII on 4K UHD, Blu-ray and Digital in the U.S. on November 10, 2026. Preorders for all three releases open September 29. The new editions include theatrical and extended or unrated cuts, with Dolby Atmos audio included with the extended versions. Saw VI and Saw VII are also presented with Dolby Vision. Released theatrically in 2008, Saw V follows Detective Mark Hoffman (Costas Mandylor) as he emerges as the apparent successor to Jigsaw’s deadly legacy. FBI Agent Peter Strahm (Scott Patterson), however, suspects Hoffman’s connection to Jigsaw runs much deeper and begins an investigation that threatens to expose his secrets. Directed by David Hackl from a screenplay by Patrick Melton and Marcus Dunstan, Saw V stars Tobin Bell, Costas Mandylor, Scott Patterson, Betsy Russell, Mark Rolston, Julie Benz, Carlo Rota and Meagan Good. The new release contains the 92-minute theatrical version and 96-minute extended version. The extended cut features English Dolby Atmos audio, while the theatrical cut includes English 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio. Additional legacy supplements include two audio commentaries, featurettes devoted to the Pendulum Trap, Cube Trap, Coffin Trap and Fatal Five, behind-the-scenes material, cast and crew interviews, trailers and TV spots. Saw VI picks up with Special Agent Strahm dead and Hoffman firmly established as Jigsaw’s successor. As the FBI closes in, Hoffman launches another deadly game targeting health-insurance executive William Easton, fulfilling one of John Kramer’s final personal wishes. Kevin Greutert directed the 2009 sequel from a screenplay by Patrick Melton and Marcus Dunstan. The cast includes Tobin Bell, Costas Mandylor, Betsy Russell, Mark Rolston, Peter Outerbridge and Shawnee Smith. The 2026 edition includes the 90-minute theatrical version and 92-minute extended version. The release features Dolby Vision, with Dolby Atmos available on the extended cut and English 5.1 DTS-HD Master Audio on the theatrical version. The extensive legacy extras include audio commentaries, Jigsaw Revealed, The Traps of Saw VI, behind-the-scenes material, director’s diaries, cast and crew interviews, music videos, trailers, TV spots and Tobin Bell answering fan questions. The seventh movie brings the battle over Jigsaw’s legacy to a head as a group of survivors turns to self-help guru Bobby Dagen (Sean Patrick Flanery). Bobby claims to have survived one of Jigsaw’s games, but secrets from his past ultimately make him the focus of another brutal series of tests. Also released as Saw: The Final Chapter, the 2010 film was directed by Kevin Greutert and written by Patrick Melton and Marcus Dunstan. Tobin Bell, Costas Mandylor and Betsy Russell return alongside Sean Patrick Flanery and Cary Elwes. Both the theatrical and extended versions run approximately 90 minutes. The new edition features Dolby Vision, while the extended cut includes English Dolby Atmos audio. Returning supplements include producer and writer audio commentaries, deleted and extended scenes, 52 Ways to Die, music videos, behind-the-scenes footage and cast and crew interviews. All three November releases pair the new 4K UHD presentations with Blu-ray and Digital copies while retaining substantial collections of bonus material from previous editions. title: Jim Abbott on his career and winning the Jimmy V Award at the ESPYs - Michigan Public
content: Flint native Jim Abbott dominated collegiate baseball at the University of Michigan before being selected eighth overall in the 1988 Major League Baseball draft. On top of being one of the best pitchers in the majors, Abbott was born without a right hand. He spent his career proving he could be a great pitcher and baseball player no matter his limb difference. More than 25 years after Abbott retired, his impact on sports is still being recognized. ESPN recently released a documentary called Southpaw: The Life and Legacy of Jim Abbott and he was awarded the prestigious Jimmy V Award at the ESPYs this July. He joined Stateside Host April Baer to talk about his career and what it means to receive the Jimmy V Award. The following is a transcript of the conversation and has been edited for length and clarity. April Baer: Did you know about the Jimmy V Award before you were under consideration for it? Jim Abbott: Well, I knew about it before the ceremony, but I was just as shocked when I got the phone call from my friend Mike Farrell at ESPN, my collaborator on the documentary that we did a couple years ago. It's an iconic award in the sports world. These are like the athletic Oscars. It's a fancy event. A lot of people getting dressed up and a lot of famous people in the audience. So my first reaction was being deeply honored. My second reaction was terror of speaking in front of the group because there have been some very, very memorable and moving, impactful speeches that were given in association with that award. AB: I watched the clip of your speech and it was wonderful. You said at one point that it's important to have focus on what's been given rather than what's been taken away. Were there times in your life when your limb difference was something that you didn't have that kind of peace with? JA: I think there was an evolution. And, you know, self-awareness comes along as we grow a little bit older. And in my case, there was always the presence of being just a little bit different whether it was on a playground or whether it was in a classroom or whether it was on a sporting field. And so there were reminders of not looking like other kids, of not being able to do things the way other kids did them. And what you find is, those things are very present when you're young. Very present. You think about them a lot and you process them a lot, but as you get older, it's almost like a muscle. You get stronger and you become more inured to it. You're used to it. You're able to deal with it and process it — and I think in a little bit healthier way. At least that was my experience. You mentioned the fact that you came up with some different methods for switching the glove back and forth, and you had a technique for balancing your mitt on your right hand while you were pitching. JA: It was an evolution. I learned to throw and catch with my dad. As a lot of people say, they were out in the front yard, just throwing the ball back and forth and just trying to figure out a way to get the glove, you know, because I couldn't throw with my right hand and I couldn't catch with my right hand. So I had to do this, do all of it with my left. It was an evolution. I can't say that it was smooth all the way through. There was a lot of trial and error. And I used to — in the same way that basketball players will tell you that they used to just go out and shoot baskets by themselves imagining the countdown at the end of the game and making that clutch shot. For me, it was baseball — I used to throw a ball against a brick wall and watch it bounce back to me and try to catch it. And I wasn't trying to practice. I wasn't trying to get better. I was just out there having fun. And I think that helped me to learn how to switch the glove on and off of my left hand. AB: There are a lot of other athletes with limb differences who've broken through at the professional level in recent years in different ways and different sports. That said, you know, the game of baseball has just gone through some changes. Do you ever think about whether it would have been possible to have had the career that you had today? JA: I marvel at the athleticism and the talent of the modern players, no question, but no, I truly believe that you can do things differently and still do them just as well as anybody else. I truly, truly believe that. And I think that goes back to the spirit of my hometown in Flint, Michigan. Parents and teachers and coaches who wouldn't take no for an answer. You know, who were bound and determined to find that way of going about things and tying shoes and buttoning a shirt and switching the glove on and off. So, yes, I firmly believe that an athlete with the talent and ability, may not be able to do it exactly the way people do it day in and day out, but I still believe they can do it just as well. I believe that is out there as a possibility. title: I use Excel all day, every day—the simple Ctrl+Shift+V shortcut saves me the most time - How-To Geek
content: I write about Excel shortcuts a lot, and I've picked up plenty over the years. Some are useful only in very specific situations. Others become so familiar that I don't even think about pressing them anymore. Since Microsoft introduced Ctrl+Shift+V to Excel in 2022, it's become one of those shortcuts for me. I've lost count of how many times I've copied something in Excel, pressed Ctrl+V, and immediately thought, "That's not what I wanted." That's because Ctrl+V can bring a lot more with it than the thing I was actually trying to copy: formulas, formatting, data validation, comments, and other cell attributes. With Ctrl+Shift+V, I can take the result and leave much of the source behind. It's especially handy when I've already spent time getting the destination looking right. I'll have a report with the exact number formats, colors, and borders I want. Then, when I paste something into it, the source formatting barges in and rearranges everything. Ctrl+Shift+V can paste the values without bringing the extra cell contents along. I also use it when I've finished calculating something and have reached the point where I want only the value. If a cell contains =H2-I2 and displays $9,237.80, I might have no reason to keep that formula once the figure has made its way into a finished report. Ctrl+Shift+V turns that result into a good old-fashioned hard-coded value. It's also useful when I need to move a spilled result in an Excel table. This is also where it saves me from a whole load of Excel baggage. Maybe the source cells have conditional formatting I don't want, or data validation that made perfect sense in the original worksheet but has no business following my data into its new home. Pasting the values means I'm taking the results rather than dragging all that stuff along with them. External links are another reason I sometimes reach for Ctrl+Shift+V. If I've built a report using formulas that pull information from another workbook, those formulas can become a headache when I send the file to someone who doesn't have the source workbook. Pasting the results as values removes those external formula dependencies, so the numbers travel with the report instead of relying on another workbook being available. If you're using Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows or Excel for the web, you can start using Ctrl+Shift+V right away. However, if you're using an older perpetual version of Excel, you'll need to rely on other methods. The right-click menu is probably the easiest alternative. If my hand is already on the mouse, there's nothing wrong with right-clicking, finding the paste option I want, and clicking it. But if I've just pressed Ctrl+C and my fingers are already on the keyboard, moving my hand over to the mouse feels like an unnecessary detour. The ribbon works in much the same way. I actually quite like the visual Paste menu, because I can hover over the various icons and see previews of what they do. Once I know I want to paste values, though, I don't need to go hunting through the ribbon for the right button. I could also use Alt > H > V > V to access the same option, but Ctrl+Shift+V gets me there in three keystrokes. Then there's Ctrl+Alt+V, which opens Paste Special. This is one of those Excel shortcuts I don't want to lose because it's also where I can paste formulas or formats, transpose data, skip blanks, perform calculations, and more. That's great when I need one of those options, but if I'm simply trying to paste a value without its formula, opening a dialog feels like bringing a toolbox to change a light bulb. I've also used the right-click-and-drag method. Select the cells, drag them somewhere else with the right-click button pressed, and when you release it, you get options ranging from copying as values or formatting to shifting cells out of the way. It's a handy little trick, because I can move the data and choose how I want it copied at the same time. But again, for pasting values, it's a long-winded way to get there. That's really why Ctrl+Shift+V has stuck with me: I don't have to stop and think about it. Copy, move to the destination (or stay in the same place if you're overwriting the copied data), press Ctrl+Shift+V, and carry on working. If you're using Excel on a Mac, the keyboard options are a little different. Excel for Mac lets you add Paste Values to the Quick Access Toolbar (QAT) or assign the command your own keyboard shortcut. Office for Mac also supports KeyTips, which let you use the keyboard to navigate commands on the ribbon and QAT. Ctrl+Shift+V might be one of the simplest Excel shortcuts I use, but it has probably saved me more time than any other. That said, it's not the only one I turn to every day. Here are some others that have also earned a permanent place in my workflow: We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. Ctrl+shift+v works virtually anywhere to paste anything you've copied to the clipboard without its original formatting. Great to know for Excel, sure, but eminently useful in all apps like simply copying and pasting web or email content which is virtually guaranteed to have special formatting. Honestly I wish "paste without formatting" was the default Ctrl+v action as I almost never want the original formatting. title: Richard "Dick" V. Klein - Herald Times Reporter
content: Richard “Dick” V. Klein, age 94, a Manitowoc resident, passed away Sunday, September 13, 2026 at his home, with his loving wife Pat at his side, on their 40th wedding anniversary. Dick was born March 8, 1932 in Manitowoc, son of the late Valentine and Mollie Klein. He attended schools in Manitowoc and graduated from Lincoln High School with the class of 1950. Following high school, Dick proudly served in the United States Marine Corps. Following his honorable discharge, he worked at the A&P store for two years then took a job with Wisconsin Electric Co. He moved to Port Washington where he became active in politics, serving two years on the county board and sixteen years as an alderman. He also served as commander of American Legion Post 82, Commander of Ozaukee Leatherneck Club, Vice President of Local 317 Operating Engineers and charter member of Christ the King Lutheran Church. In 1956 he married the former Audrey Ahrens, mother of his five children. In 1986 he married Pat (Trish) Fisher. They bought a cottage in Langlade County where they enjoyed many family get togethers as well as ATV and snowmobiling riding. They also enjoyed vocations in Biloxi, Mississippi, The Villages, Florida, and Mexico. After retiring in 1993 they moved back to Manitowoc. He was asked to join “Gramps” golf league that turned out to be a great time. One of the highlights was getting a hole-in-one. Dick is survived by the love of his life: Pat Klein; his children: Teri (Tom) Wagner, Lisa (Randy) Nothem, DeAnne “Dee Dee” (Steve) Binversie, Bob (Sherri) Klein, and Chris (Sarah) Klein; his step-children: Mike (Jill) Fisher, Mary Mattson, Tom Fisher (Jody Kunish), and Sara (John) Duzeski; his grandchildren: Adam (Emily) Nothem, Bryan Nothem, Katie Charnon (Fiancé Robbie), Taylor Wagner, Austin Wagner, Molly Klein (Marcus), Jessy Klein, Lauren Binversie (Fiancé Kyle), Rhys Klein, and James Klein; his step-grandchildren: Jason (Kirsten) Christiansen, Chad (Kate) Christiansen, Brianna Mattson, Clint Duzeski, Brent (Kasey) Duzeski, and Trisha (Alex) Vandenplas; his great-grandchildren: Trey Charnon, Londynn, Hudson, and Charlotte Christiansen, Derek, Grant, Nolin, and Koltin Duzeski, Ellie Wagner, Finley and Orrin Christiansen, and Angus Nothem. Coming from a large family, Dick is also survived by sisters: Beverley Lochka, Darlene (Don) Eisenshink, and Sandra Sprang; one sister-in-law: June Klein; one brother-in-law: Allen (Judy) Stryzewski; and two sisters-in-law: Ruth Husk and Sr. Mary Clarette Stryzewski. In addition to his parents, Dick was preceded in death by one brother and three sisters in infancy, his sisters: Bette (Joe) Sleger and Bonnie Mott; his brother: Rick Klein; brothers-in-law: Alan Petri, Jack Lochka, Rod Husk, and Roger Sprang; a son-in-law: Brent McIntyre; and a loving grandson: Eric Nothem. Cremation has occurred at the Harrigan Parkside Crematory, Manitowoc, and a memorial service will be held at 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, September 22, 2026 at St. Paul Lutheran Church, 2601 S. 10th Street, Manitowoc. Officiating at the service will be the Rev. Heather Yerion-Keck. Military honors will be accorded by American Legion Post 88 of Manitowoc. Dick will be laid to rest at Calvary Catholic Cemetery, Manitowoc, at a later date. The family will greet relatives and friends from 9:30 a.m. until the time of the service at 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, September 22, 2026 at St. Paul Lutheran Church, Manitowoc. In lieu of flowers, donations would be appreciated in Dick’s name to local veterans groups. The Harrigan Parkside Funeral Home and Crematory, Manitowoc, is assisting the family with funeral arrangements. The family wishes to extend a special thank you to their angel, nurse Nikki, who was the support they needed and the rest of the girls that took care of Dick. Thank you, HomeCare Health Services and Hospice, for the care and compassion shown to Dick and his family. Coping with grief when a traditional funeral isn't possible

title: Ford increases V-8 engine availability, lowers performance prices for 2027 F-150 trucks - CNBC
content:
DETROIT — Ford Motor is expanding the availability of V-8 engines and lowering the starting prices of some performance models for its 2027 lineup of F-150 pickup trucks. The Detroit automaker said the changes are meant to give customers more choice and help expand sales of key models, a strategy Ford has been leaning into under CEO Jim Farley. The changes come as automakers attempt to address industrywide affordability concerns. The moves are also building on some automakers — particularly the Detroit Three — adding more V-8 engines amid weakened emissions regulations and penalties under the Trump administration. The new pricing doesn’t mean the trucks are cheap. The 2027 Ford F-150 Raptor will start at $77,800, which is $4,000 less than the current truck. The 2027 Tremor will start about $5,300 lower at $62,400, Ford said Tuesday. Ford officials said the automaker lowered prices by eliminating some standard equipment, such as heated second-row seats as well as using manual instead of power controls for some parts, like the steering column. “For us, it made sense because it just broadens the offer and certainly doesn’t take away from either the capability of that new entry or of the model that it came down from,” Todd Eckert, Ford Blue senior director of truck consumer marketing, told CNBC. Regarding the V-8 availability, Ford will offer its 5.0-liter engine across every model of the F-150 lineup, Eckert said. That includes having the option for a V-8 engine in the high-end King Ranch and Platinum models for the first time since the 2023 model year. “We heard pretty loudly from both customers and dealers that even on those premium series, that they wanted the option to have a V-8 engine,” Eckert said. The changes are part of several updates the company is making to the F-150 lineup for the 2027 model year. It’s also rolling out style updates to many models and adding a Carhartt model in collaboration with the Detroit-based clothing company. All the updates for the 2027 F-150 lineup come as Ford continues to increase availability of the crucial pickups after fires at an aluminum supplier severely impacted their output over the past year. Ford’s F-Series trucks — which include the F-150 and larger “Super Duty” models such as F-250, F-350 and F-450 — were severely impacted by the supplier issues due to their large aluminum bodies and other components. title: DIABLO V Breakdown: Timeline, Storyline, Classes, and More - Nerdist
content: Alongside the reveal of the newest installment in the StarCraft franchise, the other big surprise of BlizzCon 2026 was Diablo V. On track for a 2029 release, Diablo V will bring the dark-fantasy action-RPG series to its most brutal and chaotic setting yet. It will give players plenty of incentive to tear through dangerous mobs of foes to power up with valuable loot and to take down the series’ toughest villains.During BlizzCon 2026, we got an early breakdown of what’s in store for the action-RPG series’ bold step into a dark future. Along with hearing from game director Joe Shely and narrative director Jennifer Hepler about bridging Diablo IV to V, we also got some early teases on which classes are to come with Diablo V, and how the post-apocalyptic dark fantasy adventure will change how players explore and fight in a Diablo game. With the reveal of Diablo V, we learned that the next game is set over a century after the events of Diablo IV‘s Age of Hatred saga, which saw the heroes of Sanctuary face off against Lilith and Mephisto’s dark legions. Unfortunately, the relative peace following Mephisto’s fall was short-lived, and the Prime Evil Diablo and their forces of hell launch another invasion in the realm of Sanctuary—and they ultimately succeed. With the world now in ruin following hell’s invasion, powerful heroes and the remaining survivors of Sanctuary trek across the ruins of civilization to power up and face off against Diablo once again.In Diablo V, the main story will follow a road journey of sorts, with players traveling with a caravan of other survivors through the ruined world and venturing into new, increasingly dangerous regions. All the while, Diablo’s influence will be felt throughout, and his presence in the main story will be the most front-facing of the series—even with moments where the player characters will struggle with resisting his powers.“While we were working on Diablo V, there were things we wanted to do with player agency and give you a close connection to the story of Diablo, and put you in the driver’s seat in the story,” said narrative director Jennifer Hepler. “It’s about giving you a defined identity, and those were things that we’ve been working on already while Diablo IV’s content has been coming out. When Diablo IV‘s Lord of Hatred expansion came out, we saw how much the community responded to feeling central to the story, not just a wanderer who came in. They built relationships with characters like Lilith and Mephisto. Seeing those responses felt like it really validated the approach we were doing for D5, and it definitely made me want to go full steam ahead with our approach.” The developers are also shifting away from the vast but fixed open world of D4, and back toward a more classic approach to exploration for the new entry. Along with the return of procedurally generated maps, players will also stick to a singular community of allies within the caravan, who will be your guide and quest givers. The aim for Diablo V‘s main story is to keep progression something of a surprise and to add unpredictability to the journey through a dark world, all while keeping your fragile community together. Despite the bleak tone, the developers of D5 see the game as having a hopeful message: that light can come from the darkest times.The developers also said Diablo will have the largest starting roster of classes in the series, with more to come post-launch. So far, the confirmed player D5 classes are the Demon Hunter and the Monk (returning from Diablo III), and the brand new Plague Knight class, which is a blend of a heavily armored melee fighter with a poison-spewing mage. It’s all about giving players options for how they want to fight through post-apocalyptic Sanctuary, and the developers were keen to use the successes of Diablo IV going into D5. “I would say we’re not just looking back on Diablo IV, but we’re looking alongside it,” said game director Joe Shely. “While we’ve been working on this game, we’ve been paying attention to the incredible success of things like War Plans in Diablo IV‘s Lord of Hatred, which has been incredible to see. Diablo IV has a bright future and a lot of incredible content and lessons for us.”As for Diablo IV, the developers are still aiming to deliver steady content and new updates, even with no more expansions on the way. Along with seasonal content planned for the next few years ahead of Diablo V‘s launch – with many updates building up to the main villain’s eventual plans for victory prior to D5‘s core events – Diablo IV will also see the return of the playable Amazon in 2027, which has been long overdue.So far, Diablo V is making a great case for the franchise’s sudden pivot to a new entry. For a long time, Diablo has been THE dark fantasy RPG, but to see the developers pull the lever all the way to the nightmare scenario for its next entry is a bold choice. But it’s also one that feels like it could make for the most daring game of the series. Hopefully, we’ll be able to see the true scope of this post-apocalyptic journey soon.

title: In the Hacks v Widow’s Bay Emmys battle, it’s we – the audience – who are the real winners - The Guardian
content: What’s exciting to me isn’t who took home the statue but what the creators behind these women-driven comedies will do next Emmys 2026: Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic wins Emmys 2026: red carpet looks and outfits at TV’s biggest night – in pictures There are three essential things to know about me: I love comedy, I love women and I love television. So as you can imagine, the centre of my world is women in TV comedies. Going into the 2026 Emmy awards, there was a big beautiful battle shaping up between two women-driven comedies: Hacks, a truly masterful hilarious show that just finished up with its fifth season, and Widow’s Bay, a truly original hilarious show that took us by storm with its first season. Conveniently for me, these were also my favourite two comedies of the year. The two opening awards set the stage perfectly. Supporting actress in a comedy was a stacked category, won by Kate O’Flynn, and extremely deservedly, according to me. Patricia on Widow’s Bay was my favourite new character of the year. O’Flynn played her with incredible physicality, finely honed comedic skill, and a vulnerability that made me want to cry as often as I laughed. The second award of the night, lead actress in a comedy, was equally important and equally correct. The brilliant Jean Smart of Hacks became the first woman to win the category for every season of a multi-season show. Her eighth acting Emmy, and Allison Janney’s eighth Emmy for The Diplomat, sees four women tie for the all-time record with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman. Is this because these women are particularly outstanding (yes) or is it that meaty, recurring roles like this for women are kind of rare (also yes)? Either way, it’s a huge and very deserved achievement. Smart’s portrayal of Deborah Vance is one of the great comedy performances. Deborah is complicated and powerful and selfish and occasionally monstrous but she is also vulnerable, lonely, ambitious and extremely funny. The character grew massively over the course of Hacks and Smart and the writers somehow made every version of her equally compelling. If I could have chosen anything to award jointly, it would have been writing for a comedy series, which Katie Dippold took home for Widow’s Bay. But Hacks definitely deserved a nod here too. I love the writing on the all the seasons, and I love that it was created by brilliant women and one brilliant man who thinks of women as full humans – Lucia Aniello, Jen Statsky and Paul W Downs (the W stands for “women”). Hacks never faltered in its five seasons, staying so funny and so engaging, which is hard to do in comedy. It also made a star out of Meg Stalter (I already knew she was a star but it was good for everyone else to realise). I’d never say Katie Dippold didn’t deserve the win. While it’s only had one season, Widow’s Bay’s totally unique comedic tone sets it apart. Katie Dippold (a woman) has a history of writing great comedy, from Parks and Recreation to the underrated 2013 film The Heat. With Widow’s Bay, she used all her chops to create her own world, with her own style of humour and spookiness, and she wrote great parts for older women too, like the brilliant Dale Dickey and K Callan. The script was hilarious, and so was every other aspect of the show – anyone who thinks it isn’t a comedy is straight up incorrect. But both series, as well as shows including the great Quinta Brunson’s Abbott Elementary, also nominated several times, are examples of what can happen when women are given the chance to helm comedy. The real story of the day was how exciting it was to have these brilliant shows up against each other, all these talented people in the room together. I’m happy for the winners and sad for the losers – but the important fact is that we had a year of great television. After this Emmy season, what’s most exciting to me isn’t who took home a statue but what all of these creators will get to do next. Paul W Downs has spoken about moving on to do a limited series with a tonal shift, which is thrilling news. Widow’s Bay season two is going to start shooting in March, which is, I hate to repeat myself but I must – thrilling news. Widow’s Bay may have taken the majority of the wins, including the knockout blow of best comedy, but fans of Hacks simply can’t be disappointed with how wonderfully that show played out. The Emmys are over, yes, but as fans of these shows, as supporters of these talented creatives who will go on to make more excellent television, we should remember that we, the audience, are the real winners.

title: It's 2026, And I'm Playing GTA V For The First Time - Aftermath
content: Without any nostalgia or youthful memories, Grand Theft Auto V is a strange game to experience I’ve been broadly immune from the GTA VI hype, not for any principled reasons but because I’ve just never played a Grand Theft Auto game. This has been largely circumstantial, as someone who didn’t own a console when they all released and who tends to dislike driving games. But the recent flurry of GTA VI looks got curiosity gnawing at my brain, wanting to share in the excitement of my peers and feeling drawn to a big open world to explore. And since VI won’t be coming to PC until god-knows-when, I’ve decided to do the only thing I can: finally install the copy of GTA V that’s been sitting on my computer for years. I picked up GTA V when it was free on the Epic store all the way back in 2020, my curiosity largely piqued by having spent years editing Zack Zwiezen’s stories about GTA Online for Kotaku. Zack made the game sound like a weird alternate universe full of the kind of day-to-day life management that I love about survival games, and I hoped the single-player would be that but without other players griefing me into quitting. “I could be a GTA guy,” I confidently told myself in 2020, before proceeding to never think about the game sitting in my Epic library again. A few weekends ago I finally decided to install it. This took a while: Between the Epic store being, well, itself, and my Rockstar account deciding I didn’t exist over and over until it randomly decided oh no wait I did, between account syncs that warned me they failed but didn’t seem to affect anything to having to install BattleEye, my first hour with the game was just a maze of pop-ups and error messages. Once I got into the game, though, things have run pretty smoothly. (Well, smoothly barring that it seems like the combination of using Epic and installing the game on a new SSD means that I can’t tell if my screenshots aren’t saving at all, or if they’re just being saved to some place where I have no hope of finding them. So sorry for the lack of images in this post; I didn’t realize until it was too late! Rest assured every screenshot I took was terrible anyway.) It’s weird to play a very old GTA when I’ve never played one before, and when my only reference for this style of Rockstar game is having not finished Red Dead Redemption 2. I’ve struggled a bit with the tutorials, which appear as tiny text prompts in the upper left of my screen and frequently disappear before I can internalize them. In Franklin’s first “real” mission, where he has to shoot a man fleeing on a motorbike while driving, I kept missing or misunderstanding which buttons I had to press so many times that I had to pause the game and go Google it. I then proceeded to fail the execution of this mechanic so many times that the game finally let me skip the mission, a choice I have continued to make every time the mechanic has arisen, and which I’m sure will have no consequences on my time with the rest of the game at all. Mostly what I’ve done in the game so far is wander around. I’ve only done a couple of Franklin’s missions and two of Michael’s, spending the rest of my time switching between the characters to explore their various neighborhoods. The world is definitely big–the other night I thought I was driving Michael toward one of his question mark sidequests, but when I couldn’t find it I instead walked the whole beach to the fairgrounds, rode the rides, then stole a jet ski and tried to see if I could circumnavigate the entirety of the map. Things hit a snag when I stopped to explore a little island and returned to find my jet ski had not just floated away but seemingly despawned. I stole a boat and kept going, before irrevocably beaching the boat and ending up having to walk for ages through rural dirt roads until I could find a car. A lot of my in-game time has been spent this way: stranding myself on the farthest edges of the map and having to time-consumingly work my way inland again. I also spent multiple in-game days attempting to locate a bicycle. When I discovered that I couldn’t just buy a bike from the in-game internet and store it in Michael’s garage, I wandered the streets of Los Santos hoping to come across one. Eventually I turned to the real-life internet for help, which told me bikes could be found at the beach, the only place in GTA V I can reliably navigate myself to. But I spent full nights and days skulking around parking lot bike racks hoping someone with a bike would come by while they steadfastly did not. Eventually, I walked my way to a bike rental place and nicked one there, which has led to me biking all over town in Michel’s ridiculous jeans and coat, with the current aim of getting back to a national park I passed so I can do some off-road riding. (The game is way more fun on a bike than in a car, if you ask me.) While exploring is what I most like to do in open-world games anyway, it’s also been a way to ease myself into what GTA V actually seems to be. The atmosphere is crass in a way games aren’t anymore–one of the first interactable businesses I came across was a strip club where I could watch a shiny, skimpily-dressed woman writhe in front of me. I also went to a movie, in which a cartoon robot murdered a female robot for rejecting his advances. There are poop and dick and sex and gay jokes everywhere, in a way I think most games, if they haven’t rejected them outright, are at least more artful with today. Maybe some of this was funny in 2013, but in 2026 it mostly feels embarrassing. In his 2022 re-review of the game for Polygon, Cameron Kunzelman wrote that “Back when the game originally released, I called it conservative… Now I would call it out of touch — even for the era in which it was released.” Some of the game feels like it’s trying to have its cake and eat it too, leaning on the South Park defense of making fun of everyone while still essentially being the thing it’s making fun of. There’s a crude cynicism to its humor that, looking through the lens of 2026, is hard to write off as simply dated. And it feels like it’s trying to appeal to a particular vision of “gamers” that isn’t just inaccurate today, but toxic in a different way than it was in 2013. It’s bizarre to play a game whose satirical politics are closer to the Tea Party than MAGA; even though so many of the same conspiracies and hatreds carry through, lines of thought that felt easy to write off or mock back then feel much more serious today. And it’s kind of shocking to play a game that feels like it’s both teasing and catering to a vision of an audience that was crafted before Gamergate. So many of the game’s jokes feel like Gamergate dog whistles, and I have to keep reminding myself that they can’t be, because there weren’t those dogs to whistle at when Rockstar’s developers were making the game. The elements of what would become Gamergate were there, of course; there’s a prescience to GTA V, at the same time as I think there’s no way its developers could have known precisely what they were predicting. I feel weird being disgusted by some of the game, because that reaction veers so close to the moral panics surrounding the GTA series that get wielded against video games as a whole. On the plus side, it also makes the current conservative backlash to GTA VI even more hilarious. GTA looms so large in the public imagination, and is so weight-bearing to the current video game industry, that it’s hard to experience V for the first time just as itself, to not read so much into every billboard and radio spot and activity and character. There’s so much more of it that I need to experience before I can really understand what it is and what it’s doing. But with all the baggage around it, and with what I’ve seen so far when I get too close to the game’s core, I’m not totally sure that I want to. I’ve had more fun just exploring the world, even as I keep brushing against things I think are closed to me until I advance more of the plot. I want to open up all the secrets and mysteries that Zack’s stories made sound so enticing, even as I’m worried what I might find there. GTA V is a strange game to come to without any nostalgia; I’m not quite sure if I’m enjoying it, or what it could look like to enjoy it for the first time in 2026. I would really like to get far enough to buy a better bicycle, though. Albumin is the predominant protein lost in urine during renal disease. Monitoring proteinuria through UP/C testing allows veterinarians to identify CKD early and implement treatments that can slow disease progression. title: 250. What We Learned from USPS v. California - Steve Vladeck | Substack
content: By now, you’ve probably seen the headlines—that the Supreme Court on Monday night denied the Trump administration’s application for a stay in U.S. Postal Service v. California, thereby leaving intact district court injunctions that will effectively prevent the federal government from implementing a new USPS rule respecting mail-in ballots in time for this November’s elections. Without question, this is a very big decision (and a big loss for President Trump). It’s also not an especially surprising ruling, even for this Court. As my Georgetown colleague Marty Lederman documented in multiple blog posts, and as a really excellent amicus brief by Professors Rick Hasen, Ned Foley, Pam Karlan, and Doug Laycock demonstrated in detail, the government had (and made) both an exceptionally weak case on the merits and an even weaker case on the “equities” of emergency relief—even relative to other emergency applications that, in my view, should also have been denied. And although the Court wrote only three sentences (sigh), two of those sentences signaled the majority’s agreement on both of those points: “The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction. And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor a stay.” Just to say it out loud, those are two independently fatal obstacles to relief. But despite the (unfortunate) brevity of the Court’s order, I wanted to write a quick post about the decision because I think we still learned at least three important lessons from the nine pages the justices handed down last night—one about the majority; one about Justice Kavanaugh (who wrote a one-paragraph concurrence); and one about Justices Thomas and Alito (who filed an eight-page dissent penned by Alito). A lot of media outlets reported the ruling as 7-2. As ever, I think that’s a mistake—not because it’s necessarily wrong, but because it isn’t necessarily right. It seems to me that we only know three things for a fact: First, Justices Thomas and Alito were publicly in dissent. Second, Justice Kavanaugh was publicly in the majority. And third, at least five other justices were also in the majority (because of the daylight between the majority’s cryptic sentence on the merits and what Justice Kavanaugh wrote in his concurrence, about which more shortly). Math being math, that leaves the possibility that a third justice voted for the stay internally, but chose not to make their views public—that it was 6-3, not 7-2. We won’t know (for a long time) if this happened, and it’s almost certainly a distinction without a meaningful difference in the interim. But as with so many things about the Court’s emergency docket, it’s important to distinguish between what we know and what we think. To me, the more significant math point here is that there’s no way it was 5-4. And so despite Justice Kavanaugh’s (surprising) support for the USPS’s authority here, my own read of the cryptic order is that five other justices publicly signaled that they do not believe the government will ultimately succeed in challenging Judge Talwani’s injunction. If that was all the Court had written, it would be possible to interpret that as a point about the equities—that five justices believed the government would never be able to displace preliminary relief in this case (which, again, would make sense given the imbalance of the equities here, and would not necessarily be expressing a view on the validity of the USPS rule). But given that the Court added a separate sentence about the equities, it sure seems to me that a majority of the Court wanted to signal something bigger—that the government isn’t going to win this case, because it’s unlikely five justices will ultimately vote to sustain the USPS rule even “on the merits.” If so, that’s a really important message not just to the Trump administration, but to lower courts. Unlike the Missouri redistricting dispute from last week, this case surely will go forward. And for better or worse (and my own view is the former), five justices other than Justice Kavanaugh have now put a pretty heavy thumb on the scale against the government on the merits. Justice Kavanaugh, once again to his credit (I’ve been consistent about this), wrote separately to explain his position. Taking out his citations, here’s what he said: In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority. But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections. For that reason, I concur in the denial of the application for stay. Again, there’s a lot going on in three short sentences. The first sentence sure reads like a response to the majority—that, unlike his five (or six) colleagues who also voted to deny the stay, he thinks the USPS may win on the ultimate merits of the validity of the rule. If this is a response to the majority, then I think it only reinforces the reading that the majority was suggesting exactly the opposite. For what it’s worth, I think he’s completely wrong on the merits. But the fact that he felt impelled to make that point is at least decent evidence that the majority thinks so, too. The second sentence is what I find most striking. I would’ve thought that the fact that “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections” is an argument about the equities—that, even if the government is likely to ultimately prevail, the harms and chaos from rushing the rule into effect are reason enough to keep the rule paused through November. But Justice Kavanaugh frames it as a procedural APA violation instead. That matters in at least two respects. First, Kavanaugh may be avoiding the equities because otherwise he’d have to explain why Purcell doesn’t push in exactly the opposite direction—since he has so often deployed that “principle” to keep federal courts from doing exactly what Judge Talwani did here, i.e., blocking an eleventh-hour legislative/executive change to voting rules. Second, and Purcell aside, this approach seems to open the door to other challenges to late-breaking federal changes to election procedures on procedural APA grounds—where the argument is that the change is procedurally unlawful because it is so late in the game. At least off the cuff, that seems like an interesting way to convert the malleability of equities balancing in election cases into more objective procedural harms, at least when the federal government is the defendant. But smarter folks than me will need to think about how that can and would work in practice. I have been quite critical before of many of Justice Alito’s separate opinions on the emergency docket. He has a tendency to take liberties with the facts (or procedural posture); to make brazen claims without substantiation; and to insinuate unclean hands on the part of lower courts, litigants, and/or his colleagues in the majority without doing the work of proving it. Well, all of those tendencies were on display in these eight pages, along with a rather stunning disregard for the interests of eligible voters in having their lawfully cast votes counted. Indeed, to the concern that the rule would disenfranchise millions of voters, Alito’s only response was that “I take that problem very seriously, but it is not enough to convince me to deny the application.” Why not? Alito offered two reasons, and they’re both remarkably tendentious. First, Alito wrote that “the States disagree about the nature of these effects. Twelve States supported the rule below and asserted that compliance at this time is practicable.” As Professor Derek Muller explains in a lengthy post over at Election Law Blog, this is (1) a remarkable tense-change to muddy what twelve red states actually argued below; and (2) a non-sequitur given that the ability to comply with the rule is radically different from whether that compliance will lead to massive disenfranchisement of eligible voters. Second, and worse, Alito wrote that “the plaintiff States and the courts bear a substantial share of the blame for the rule’s timing.” As the Brits would say, this is utter bollocks. Alito tried to spin the plaintiffs’ litigation behavior and the district court’s rulings as preventing the government from moving forward in putting out the USPS rule, but that’s just not a fair summary of the record. As Rick Hasen pointed out last night, “the district court allowed USPS to keep working on its rule and its (still nonexistent) portal for voluntary use by states.” Indeed, the fact that the USPS issued the rule the Supreme Court refused to unblock last night while the executive order was still enjoined should be all of the proof anyone needs that Alito is wrong to insinuate otherwise, to say nothing of the government’s inability to get the critical electronic portal online before voters started … voting. (For all of the ugly shots folks on the right have taken at Judge Talwani, the denial of a stay is a pretty significant vindication of her rulings in these cases.) Alito also blamed his colleagues, noting that “this Court spent from late July to the end of August drafting nearly 40 pages of opinions, including two dissents, despite the Government’s public notice that it would not publish a final rule while subject to the injunctions, and its representation that it had a strong interest in issuing its rule in early- to mid-August to allow time to implement it.” As Alito concluded (read this sentence carefully), “The plaintiff States cannot claim the timing of the rule tilts the equities in their favor when they, and courts hearing their claims, are responsible for so much of the delay.” Of course, it is ludicrous to blame plaintiffs for delays Alito attributes to courts. It’s even more ludicrous to do so when the Supreme Court’s own prior ruling in this case (which Alito almost certainly joined) asserted that the earlier injunctions had to be stayed because the plaintiffs’ suits were filed too early. And it’s tendentious to the extreme to claim that the point that putatively “tilts the equities in [plaintiffs’] favor” is the timing of the USPS rule, not the massive disenfranchisement that neither the government nor Alito ever publicly disputed would occur were it to go into effect. It may not surprise anyone that this is where Alito and Thomas are. But it’s striking to see it captured in writing so plainly and unmistakably. In the end, it’s heartening that only two justices were willing to say these things out loud. And it’s even more heartening that a majority of the Court was unwilling to abide President Trump’s transparent effort to make it harder for a large number of lawfully registered voters to actually cast their ballots in the 2026 general election. But it continues to be deeply sobering that it came to all of this in the first place. One First is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, please consider becoming a free or paid subscriber: A bullet dodged…for now. But The absence of a written opinion by the court means we do not know the basis for their decision….it leaves the issue open for 2028. I fear gorsuch and Barrett agree with Kavanaugh and believe the post office has authority to issue these rules under its general powers , but implementation so close to the ‘26 election is arbitrary and capricious. The notion that “there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority” is rubbish, but the comment lays down a marker that shan’t be ignored. The statutory power under 39 U.S. Code § 401 (2) to “adopt …such rules and regulations, not inconsistent with this title, as may be necessary in the execution of its functions” does not extend to determining who is and is not allowed to vote. Congress MUST pass an amendment to 39 U.S. Code § 401 expressly prohibiting the post office from issuing these regs and mandating that the post office must deliver all mailed ballots , without exception…and must postmark each as first class mail and deliver to the registrar of voters within 3 days of receipt. Otherwise, we will see these restrictions in place in 2028 Another thing we learn is that Justice Kavanaugh is a follower, not a leader. He is positioning himself to be on the right side of this case when it comes back around, whatever that turns out to be by saying "I can be had. I swing.". His basis for taking up this position is patently insufficient and consequently devoid of merit. A "plausible argument", "reasonable case to be made" or whatever he called it, for the Postal Service does not measure up to any standard at all. It means nothing. The Postal Service is not in the business of governing. It is a government corporation, in effect, like Amtrak, or Freddie Mac. It is entirely a creature or law and has only those powers and duties vested with it by the statutes that in effect constitute its corporate charter. That is what Kavanaugh was referring to as providing the plausible authority and justification for these rules. It is what the Postal Service stood on. And it is all pure boiler plate. It says nothing about regulating ballots or other articles of mail related to elections.

title: Diablo V Has a Clear Vision, and the Devs Are Confident in 2029 - PlayDayOne
content: Blizzard tells us about Diablo V's story, release date, hopes, console plans and a whole lot more At BlizzCon 2026, I was fortunate enough to be part of a group interview with some of the development team behind the just-announced Diablo V. They were asked about a variety of subjects, from the reason why the game is starting after we “lose”, to class philosophy, to console plans, to bringing in new players and a whole lot more. The three panel members were Joe Shely, Senior Game Director on Diablo, Jennifer Brandes Hepler, Narrative Director on Diablo, and Matt Zitterman, Executive Director on Diablo. I’ve paraphrased their responses below, so only words in quotes are, well, direct quotes from one of the three panel members. For the most part, the exact questions asked are omitted as I opted to use context in their answers to provide that information. Now, without further ado, let’s dive in. One of the most controversial aspects of the Diablo V announcement is the revelation that we lose! The game is set roughly a hundred years after the defeat of Mephisto in Diablo IV, and after so many years of peace, the Lord of Terror himself reappears. “What happens if you weren’t there?” That’s the reasoning they gave behind Diablo finally obtaining victory. A group of heroes rose up, as they always do, but this time they didn’t succeed. This entire premise is a creative decision that they’ll be playing off of in many ways throughout the game. The world of Diablo V is one where Diablo has ruled Sanctuary for seven full years, meaning we’re going to be playing essentially a post-apocalyptic version of the world we all know and love. When asked why they chose to take the story in such a drastic direction, they responded that the Eternal Conflict is exactly that: eternal. Sometimes evil wins, and sometimes good wins. After Diablo 4, players understood specifically what a wildcard humanity is in this conflict, and so they really wanted to play around with that concept. More specifically, they wanted to tell a story with Diablo at the centre, and they wanted a premise that would have him on display right from the start. To them, Diablo is much more terrifying when he’s more than just a hulking brute, and so they wanted to highlight his more sinister and devious side too. Interestingly, they highlighted how the angels in this conflict weren’t exactly holding up their side of the bargain, and this shift of balance might have quite a bit to do with their years of inaction. We’ll have to wait for more information there! So all this “we lost” stuff sounds pretty dour, almost too much so. The panel was asked exactly that, if this whole premise isn’t too depressing. They answered saying the exact opposite. They call the story and setting of Diablo V a very “hopeful” one, because it begins from the worst possible place. The world is already over, everything sucks, and the only place to go is up. This makes Diablo V a story of rebuilding and recovery, where you “claw back space for humanity with your fingernails.” So yes, the world itself is very dark, but they let your character, your companions, and your found family be a shining light in the darkness. Which brings us nicely to the next major change in Diablo V: the removal of towns in place of a roaming caravan. Diablo is a franchise that’s known for having various hub towns that serve as your home base of sorts in different parts of the game. Or at the very least, safe areas where you’re not being swarmed by demons left and right. Diablo V does away with all of that, and instead your home base is a constantly growing and moving caravan, a “point of light,” as they put it. Jennifer specifically mentioned how there was always a bit of disconnect between demons and monsters going crazy not two feet away from a town gate, but the town itself was completely peaceful, with demons “waiting on their schedule.” So they pitched a version of Sanctuary where there is no safe place except for the one you create. They consider this a very “pure” version of Diablo, and I’m starting to come around to it too. They also mentioned how this lets them make the characters you recruit into the caravan “real”, with “stories of their own.” Interestingly, they used the words “gives you something to lose” when referring to them too. As a player, you usually know that you’re not going to lose this next fight, but a good story should make you afraid to lose something, and they specifically mention a community that you built as that potential something to lose. It’s apparently also the shortest route every time from town portal to blacksmith! When asked how this approach would affect the endgame, or replaying areas, they assured us that you can absolutely go back and play things again. While yes, you’re a force with growing power, you’re not exactly saving the world instantly. As a mobile point of light, once you leave an area, the darkness settles back in. In terms of a post-campaign state, they mentioned how the game needs to leave you in a position where you’ve achieved something, but there’s still plenty to do. Hence, creating an integration between the campaign and endgame. I mentioned how dark the game seems before, and the caravan is another place where they want to contrast that. A campfire is something full of hope and community, and this community aspect is something they kept mentioning. Specifically, they want some of that older style of campfire storytelling in the game, not companions whose gear you change, but characters you follow, travel with, and bond with throughout the journey. The last thing they touched on in this Diablo V interview is that this whole concept of starting a journey with just a few people helps the gameplay progression of starting from nothing and building your strength up. Moving away from a fixed map is a big departure from Diablo IV, and it’s a very purposeful decision. The entire game is being built procedurally; as for why, they said it was based on what they found players enjoyed in D4. Specifically, they noticed players had a ton of fun unfurling the map of the open world, but that experience was “one and done”. To give players that feeling of constant discovery is one of the reasons for this change. When asked how they’d avoid having the maps feel repetitive too quickly, their immediate answer was “we’re going to build a lot of content.” But they also talked about how each area of the world will still have its own identity, so even though the maps themselves are procedurally generated, what you’re seeing or exploring is going to be very intentional. Expanding on this a bit, they mentioned how a map will differ based on which commander Diablo has stationed in that area. Things like the kind of tiles, monsters, and even treasure can vary due to this. An example they gave was that you may come across the same ruined church, but the way in which it is might vary. Alongside confirming that the game will ship with an overlay map at launch, they expressed pride in their procedural map-generation tech and will dive more into the specifics “at a later time.” During the interview, the team talked about how Diablo V is set to have more classes at launch than any other Diablo game. They even expressed how you can do the math how you want to, but Diablo V will still have more. I wasn’t able to confirm if this meant it would launch with more classes than, say, Diablo Immortal has right now, which is 10, but they sounded pretty confident either way. As of now, we have three confirmed classes. Two returning ones from Diablo 3, the Demon Hunter and the Monk, and a brand new one: The Plague Knight. When asked if the classes themselves would also appear darker to match the narrative, they told us that they want the classes to have different aspects on this scale. As in some classes that lean more towards darkness, like the new Plague Knight, and some that lean more towards the light, such as the Monk. One of their reasons for having so many classes is to make sure that anyone coming into the game, regardless of which Diablo game they played in the past, has something familiar waiting for them. Such as someone who only played Diablo 3 in the past would immediately recognize the Demon Hunter, who will feel and look familiar but will still have its own new aspects. So the big elephant in the room during this interview was the release date being more than two years away, and of course they were asked directly about this. They instantly responded with a “We’re very confident in hitting that date”, and then repeated what felt like a mantra that said confidence comes from their “clarity of creative vision and clarity of production schedule”. They called themselves a Diablo team that’s been making Diablo games “for a very long time” and mentioned how Diablo V is being built on top of the foundation built on Diablo IV. This allowed them to start work on this game in parallel with the other, and also let them think ahead to D5 while they worked on D4. A big part of why they announced the game this early is that they want to be able to start conversations with players on many, many things (they mentioned potential stat requirements on equipment as an example of this). They also want to develop the game in a way that they can show players more of the game even early on in development. They specifically mentioned bringing players on to campus even. This would allow them to have conversations on many topics, such as classes and characters, and let them obtain feedback early enough in development so that they have time to really change and improve things as needed. They also mentioned that one of the best ways to make a game better is to simply play it. A lot. Basically, they wanted to be able to get player feedback much earlier, and now they can openly talk about things behind the scenes. They also mentioned that of course they’ll want to get some hands-on feedback too. Asked about how some people feel discontent about another Diablo game being announced so soon while they’re still playing Diablo IV, the panel responded by saying there will continue to be “incredible reasons to keep playing Diablo IV.” They highlighted the upcoming Amazon class and the Season of Hell’s Legacy. Their words were, “There will continue to be incredible support for that game as we announce more things.” I asked them directly if Diablo V is being built as an always-online game, and they gave the same answer to someone who asked about the multiplayer plans. “We’ll have more details to share about multiplayer as we move forward.” So pretty much a non-answer, but I expected as much. Though they did say that, just like Diablo IV, the content in Diablo V will be able to be played either solo or with a group. They had a couple more non-answers, one of which was when asked about which platforms they plan to release the game on. “No specific platforms to announce right now”, was what they said, but they also followed that up with “we want as many people to play Diablo V as possible.” Of course, with the game 30 or so months out, we won’t know exact console platforms yet, but I’d say it’s a fairly safe bet that the game will be coming to both Xbox and PlayStation consoles. Someone asked them bluntly if the Diablo IV level scaling system would return, and their immediate response was that they’re not talking about that just yet. But they expanded by saying Diablo is, in many ways, a game that’s about your character growing stronger, and so when monsters get stronger outside of your control, that can get in the way of this. Their exact words were that they would “take a somewhat different approach”. When asked about the upcoming animated TV Show with Netflix, they simply said: “When the time is right, we’ll talk about more here.” Though they did mention that Diablo as a property has plenty of stories to tell. When asked if they were worried about new players being scared away by the five in the title, they mentioned how, at a high level, Diablo V is a fairly simple premise. You’re the heir to Westmarch, and there’s someone sitting on your throne. Though that someone just so happens to be the Lord of Terror, Diablo. They know that the gameplay, control scheme, and the camera angle of the game are all also very approachable. So as long as they do their job of introducing players into the depths the game has properly, they’re confident that Diablo V will be an easy game to get into even as a brand new player to the franchise. They also talked about how the big time skip and the general mystery behind how or why this all happened will help put every player on a level playing field, at least going in. Finally, they touched on how Diablo V is returning to their roots in many ways, such as having familiar classes, which will make it so any player who’s played a Diablo in the past would still find aspects of V familiar and welcoming. That’s it! There was quite a bit they touched on here in this Diablo V interview, from potential console plans to level scaling, to narrative choices, to class identity and more. Diablo V still has years until it releases, so I’m sure plenty of the above might change or be altered as time goes by, but what did you think of their answers?
