title: In Tulum, V Taller Inverts the Symbolism of the Tower of Babel - Metropolis Magazine
content: Join us every second Tuesday of the month for a dose of optimism with thought-provoking guests who are revolutionizing their fields. Innovators will lead virtual workshops for an hour of discovery, inspiration, and community. Led by editor in chief, Avinash Rajagopal, these workshops will be guided by our audience, where questions are not only welcome but encouraged. Metropolis Editors, Natural Habitat, sustainability, sustainable architecture METROPOLIS Introduces Natural Habitat, a Sustainable Homes Video Series The series debuts with a tour of a tranquil upstate New York retreat designed with Passive House principles. Mexican architects V Taller reconcile housing for tourists and long-term residents with urban chaos at the edge of the rapidly developing Mayan jungle. In the Biblical story of the Tower of Babel, the Babylonians create a winding ziggurat that climbs up to celestial heights, but in their quest to conquer nature, denizens are confronted by a chaotic multitude of languages that bring them back to earth. In the Babel residential development in Tulum, Mexico, by contrast, the tower becomes a restorative place at the center of a series of arched volumes containing multifamily housing. The architects at V Taller, based in Guadalajara and Mexico City, created a calm, healing environment that reconnects the site to the Mayan jungle. “For us, it was a search to harmonize the architecture, the landscape, the experience, the light, and the noise, using all of the tools we have as architects to transform the space and the context,” says Miguel Valverde, the firm’s codirector. The site had already been clear-cut when a developer friend from architecture school began discussing the idea with him, focusing on arches as a design feature. V Taller responded with two elbow-shaped structures composed of arcaded volumes wrapped around a courtyard with a central tower. Lushly landscaped with native plants, the development includes 59 studio or two-bedroom apartments for long- and short-term rental. The apartments, each covered by a set of arches, extend from front to back, accentuating airflow and openness. The staircases are situated in apertures between every four arches. Workshops in Guadalajara produced much of the wood furniture, which was specified in collaboration with the interior design studio Carlos y Pablo. Part of V Taller’s strategy involved isolating the interiors and courtyard from the noise of the street, influenced by the team’s exhaustion with car-centric planning and the lack of green space in their native Guadalajara—an urban design bug gradually overtaking Tulum. The predominant building material, a plaster-and-resin composite tinted light brown, provides a sense of visual unity and relaxation. “We thought that the best strategy to create silence and reduce noise was to go with a single material for the floors, walls, and ceilings and for the roof and exterior to all be the same so that the eye can rest,” says codirector Daniel Villanueva. Inside the central tower, a round reflecting pool creates a meditative space that cools its surroundings. Within the landscaped courtyard are a coworking space, a restaurant, the pool, a steam room modeled after a Turkish hammam, and a hot tub with an angular, double-height ceiling that gestures toward the sky. The feeling is of an urban oasis possessing a genuine sense of place, differentiated from the chaotic development surging up around it. “The important thing for us is to keep in mind that we are creating the next places, cities, towns, destinations,” says Valverde. “From the client to the development to the architect, all of us are responsible for the things we are creating in this society.” Would you like to comment on this article? title: The clock may be ticking on small-school football in Section V | Exclusive - Democrat and Chronicle
content: AVON – Less than 40% of Section V member schools field their own varsity football team. Merged programs dominate headlines. Small-school football resembles nothing of its former self. Class D now features just five single-school teams. It will reach four when Red Jacket co-operates with Midlakes in 2027. Andy Englert’s Avon staff watched everything change first-hand. Their schedule once consisted of LeRoy, Caledonia-Mumford, Letchworth, Warsaw and Perry. Those five schools now form two teams. Eight-man football once appeared to be the future. It now sits dormant within Section V. Declining participation numbers have reshaped Section V football in recent years. Two or three-school teams are now commonplace, including what were once the area’s greatest small school rivals. But football still thrives in some rural pockets of Section V. These programs haven’t just preserved tradition – they’ve overcome a trend sweeping high schools across the United States. What happens when numbers finally fall short? Will they be left out of the co-operative arms race, return to 8-man football, or add to the growing pile of teams whose names are hyphenated? Answering that question could define football’s future in this region. Canisteo-Greenwood graduates roughly 80 students each year. It still fields three levels of interscholastic football. Clyde-Savannah holds court to the north. Attica, a Class B or C school in most sports, plays football in ‘D’ beside Avon and Red Jacket. Twelve schools comprise the other six members of Class D. Twenty-four schools make 13 teams in Class C. Even large schools have co-opted in Section V, such as Aquinas/RACS in AA. The list grows annually. Others have resisted. Low numbers, Englert said, were a concern when he arrived at Avon in 1998. Numbers remain limited at a school such as Avon, where graduation statistics rival Canisteo-Greenwood. But the Riverhawks have thrived under Englert, who this season relinquished head coaching duties to longtime offensive coordinator Justin Dueppengiesser. “It’s the old-school mentality,” Englert said. “Let’s do it as long as we can just ourselves. We try to find guys who might not play other sports – come get involved with us.” Numbers don’t lie. After three years of rebuilding, Avon is 154-81 with seven Section V championships since 2001, including Class D titles in 2024 and 2025. “(Englert) talks to kids in the hallways and gets them excited about football,” said longtime Avon defensive coordinator Mike McGough. “It’s just as important when you have those down years that you don’t quit or look for an easy way out. We just had to stay the course and get the numbers back up to rebuild.” Successful rebuilds brought Red Jacket and Canisteo-Greenwood back to 11-man football after detours into 8-man play. C-G even features a junior varsity team this fall. “We want everyone to learn and love the game of football,” said Canisteo-Greenwood head coach Bill Drake. “But also have fun and learn to be better people in the game of life. That’s small-town football.” Drake hails from Hornell, where – despite a current high school enrollment roughly 30% larger than C-G – the Raiders began a football co-op with Arkport/Canaseraga in 2024. Predicting precisely when varsity numbers will fall short proves a difficult proposition. Red Jacket, therefore, acted while it could. Red Jacket enjoyed two Section V titles in 8-man football. Increased numbers prompted the Cardinals’ return to 11-man play in 2025, a “huge success,” according to head coach Josh Henninger. Why, then, co-op with rival Midlakes? This reunion began at youth and modified levels in 2026 and will unite the schools’ varsity programs in 2027. “We are honestly just looking ahead at projected numbers,” Henninger said. “We want to be forward-thinking so that we’re not stuck and don’t have to scrap (football).” Dwindling youth football participation and declining district populations present a twofold challenge. A 2024 study by Cornell University’s Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy projected that New York could experience a 13% population decline by 2050, with Finger Lakes and Southern Tier regions both seeing losses. This reality has spurred most to act. Co-ops have saved many programs, but they’re not perfect. “Anyone who thinks it’s as easy as adding 45 graduates at Oakfield-Alabama plus 30 graduates at Elba, it’s not that clean of a math equation,” said Oakfield-Alabama/Elba coach Tyler Winter, who doubles as Elba’s director of athletics. “I would love to be a presence in the O-A building but don’t have that luxury.” Winter started his career at York/Pavilion, one of the area’s first football co-ops. Unlike OAE – which combined two storied football programs – that merger saw York absorb a non-football school. Marcus Whitman did the same with Bloomfield in 2019 under Bruce Wagner, now the head coach at Midlakes. Community concerns, Wagner said, don’t outweigh the threat of dropping football. “It’s people from days gone by who don’t want to lose (Midlakes’) Carolina blue and black,” Wagner said. “But the writing is on the wall – either you merge, or you lose your program. I can’t even explain how bad that would be for both of us.” Like at Red Jacket, 8-man football helped OAE overcome early struggles. The Aggies won 8-man sectional titles in 2018 and 2019 before claiming Class D crowns in 2022 and 2023. Five teams played in Section V’s most recent 8-man season (2024): Red Jacket, Bolivar-Richburg (now combined with Cuba-Rushford and Portville in Section VI), Holley (combined with Lyndonville), Pembroke (combined with Alexander) and Wellsville (combined with Genesee Valley/Belfast). “I just hope that everyone involved is doing their best to preserve the game,” said Winter, also Section V’s football chairman. “Life for a teenage kid can be effortless because the whole world is at their fingertips. Whatever we can do to give kids the chance to play football the correct way, I support whatever that looks like.” Dueppengiesser’s Avon tenure begins in a familiar spot. He’s seen numbers fluctuate throughout his 17 years on staff. Standards, though, have not changed as the Riverhawks seek their first Section V three-peat this fall. Englert, though no longer head coach, will continue recruiting Avon High School hallways as director of athletics. He'll confront that question if the day ever comes. “Somebody will always want to dance with you,” Englert said. “If it gets to that point we’ll figure it out. Right now, we’re lucky to have just us.” Community support, multi-sport athletes and program culture drive programs such as Avon. Things can change quickly, though. Just ask Mynderse, which planned to play in Class D this season before low preseason numbers left it in a Class B co-op with Waterloo. Wilson/Early College, citing low numbers, won’t play a varsity season this fall. “It’s going to come, at some point, for all the smaller schools,” Henninger said. “It’s an issue that each district will need to look at and evaluate themselves.” Geography proves a challenge for schools such as Canisteo-Greenwood, one of just 13 districts in spacious Steuben County. Clyde-Savannah, the smallest Section V football school by enrollment, is one of three Wayne County programs still playing solo. The future of small-school football in Section V remains unclear. For now, survival trumps all. “It seems more districts are welcoming whatever gives kids the chance to play the most appropriate level of football they can,” Winter said. “If anything, it’s going to grow. Anyone still resistant to it might as well buckle up for the ride.” Jeff Uveino joined the USA Today Network in 2023 and began covering Rochester-area high school sports in 2026. He is a graduate of St. Bonaventure University's Jandoli School of Communication and native of Perry. Contact him at juveino@usatodayco.com. Follow him on X @realjuveino and on Instagram @jeffusports.

At IBC 2026, we spoke with Ivan Kwok at the DigitalFoto booth about the new DigitalFoto x PHOTOOLEX VB79, a co-branded 79.2Wh V-mount battery designed for camera rigs, lights, monitors, and mobile production. The battery supports up to 500W total output, includes a retractable USB-C cable, and offers multiple USB-C, USB-A, D-Tap, DC, and BP connections in a compact body. DigitalFoto is presenting the VB79 as its first V-mount battery, developed together with PHOTOOLEX, with both brands appearing on the product itself. The design is deliberately smaller and more portable than a conventional block-style V-mount, with the companies targeting content creators and smaller crews that still need the flexibility of a professional battery system. Ivan said the size answers who is buying V-mount power now. A V-mount battery, as he put it, “should be a portable and small size so that it’s easy to carry,” which explains the 79Wh starting point rather than the usual 99Wh or 150Wh. The published figures put the pack at 119 x 69 x 43mm (4.69 x 2.72 x 1.69in) and 521g (18.4oz), with a rated capacity of 79.2Wh from 5500mAh at 14.4V. That also keeps the battery under the 100Wh threshold airlines generally apply to lithium-ion packs carried in hand luggage, which removes the approval step larger V-mount batteries usually require. The headline output number is 500W. Ivan said the battery can supply that across its connections at the same time, including the 7-pin port, and he was direct about the limit that comes with it: at that draw, a 79Wh pack will last around ten minutes. The arithmetic is consistent, since 79Wh divided by 500W works out at slightly under ten minutes before the cells are empty. He positioned the higher-capacity models due later as the ones that make sustained high-draw work practical, suggesting that half an hour or an hour at that kind of load becomes possible once the capacity goes up. For now, the 500W rating is best understood as a peak the battery can handle rather than a figure anyone will run against for a full setup day. The most unusual feature is a retractable magnetic USB-C cable built into the front of the battery, extending to 50cm (19.7in) and pulling back into the body when it is not in use. Ivan said it is rated at 100W in both directions, so it can run or charge a device such as a laptop, and it can also be used as a power input to charge the battery itself. The Photoolex listing gives the same 100W figure for the cable in both directions. The top of the battery carries the rest of the connections along with mounting points, including a 1/4″-20 thread with ARRI locating holes, so the pack can be attached directly to a rig rather than only to a V-mount plate. On the power side, there is a DC output at 12V and a second at 8.4V, plus USB-A and two USB-C ports running at different levels. Ivan identified the yellow USB-C port as the 100W connection and the second USB-C port as a 36W output, which puts the 100W figure in line with the retractable cable at the front. PHOTOOLEX rates the USB-A output at 22.5W, the D-Tap at up to 200W, and the 7-pin connector at up to 500W, which is where the headline figure comes from. Charging can go through four different routes, which is unusual for a battery of this size. The yellow USB-C port accepts power in, the D-Tap can be used as a charging input, the retractable USB-C cable works as an input as well, and the 7-pin connector on the V-mount interface can charge the battery through a compatible plate or charger. Two of those can be used at once. Ivan gave the example of running the retractable cable and the USB-C port together to bring the charge time down, which matters more on a small pack that is likely to be topped up between setups rather than cycled overnight in a rack charger. PHOTOOLEX lists the combined USB-C input ceiling at 140W, with the D-Tap and 7-pin inputs rated at up to 135W each. A screen on the front shows the remaining capacity as a percentage. Holding the button for three seconds rotates the readout, so the display can be flipped between horizontal and vertical depending on how the battery is mounted, which is a small thing that matters when a pack ends up on its side on a cage or a stand. There is also a companion app. According to Ivan, it reports the number of charge and discharge cycles the battery has been through, an estimate of how long it will keep working under the current load, the remaining capacity percentage, the internal temperature, and live voltage and current figures. Cycle count and cell temperature are the kind of data that rental houses and anyone managing a set of batteries tend to want, and they are increasingly appearing on packs at this size rather than only on larger professional models. A silver button on the side operates a light built into the battery. Ivan described it as a mounting aid for dark environments, where lining a V-mount pack up with the plate by feel is awkward. A short press switches the light on, and pressing the button again turns it off. Ivan quoted a price of around €140 ($160) at the show, with availability from the end of September. Both the black and white versions use the same battery, with no difference beyond the finish. Larger capacities are planned before the end of the year. Ivan mentioned a 158Wh model and a second, larger pack above 200Wh, which would extend the line well past the airline-friendly size the range starts with. Does a V-mount battery this small earn a place in your kit, or do you want the capacity of a full-size brick? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below! title: The “born free and equal” clauses and the noxious Buck v. Bell - SCOTUSblog
content: This is the fifth of seven introductory articles on the relevance for constitutional law and the Supreme Court of the “born free and equal” clauses, which appeared in the Declaration of Independence and in six out of 12 state constitutions when the federal Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, in 24 out of 37 state constitutions when the 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868, and is in 37 out of 50 state constitutions today. The “born free and equal” clause of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, for example, provided that: In my initial articles, I showed that the “born free and equal” idea is deeply rooted in American history and tradition as that phrase is used in such correctly decided cases as Washington v. Glucksberg (rejecting a right to assisted suicide), McDonald v. City of Chicago (recognizing that the Second Amendment’s right to own a handgun for self-protection extends to the states), and Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (overturning Roe v. Wade). In the second and third article, I argued that while the 14th Amendment does not give rise to a “right to privacy,” it does through the privileges or immunities clause constitutionalize the “born free and equal” clauses, subject to rational basis review, which justifies the outcome, although not the opinions in 1965’s Griswold v. Connecticut (holding that states may not criminalize the use of contraceptives by married couples) and in 2003’s Lawrence v. Texas (holding that states may not criminalize same-sex “sodomy”). And in my fourth article, I examined the application of the “born free and equal” clauses to yet another famous “right to privacy” case: 2015’s decision in Obergefell v. Hodges, which correctly found a national constitutional right to same-sex civil marriages. Today I turn to one of the most atrocious rulings in Supreme Court history: the 1927 case of Buck v. Bell, in which the court, 8-1, upheld a model eugenics statute. Specifically, a Virginia act allowed the compulsory sterilization, for the supposed “protection and health of the state,” of anyone who was deemed by a “social worker” to have genes resulting in feeblemindedness, unfitness, or an intellectual disability. Only a perfunctory hearing was allowed to those who were compulsorily sterilized. This statute did not come out of nowhere. Rather, such eugenics laws were first championed in 1883 by the social Darwinist Sir Francis Galton, a second cousin of Charles Darwin who chillingly believed that there were many different human “races” on the earth and that those races of human beings were competing for what psychologist and philosopher Herbert Spencer called “the survival of the fittest.” Galton, who was fascinated by the concept of animal breeding of dogs and racehorses, dreamed of applying this to human beings so as to promote the most intelligent, physically strong, and beautiful or handsome of them. (Darwin himself had hinted at such an idea in “The Origin of Species,” and mentioned it in his 1871 book “The Descent of Man.”) Support for eugenics laws became an orthodox staple of the creed of the Progressive Era. In one letter, President Theodore Roosevelt stated that: Woodrow Wilson, the other major Progressive politician of the first part of the 20th century, signed a eugenics bill into law as governor of New Jersey. Other famous eugenicists included William Howard Taft; Margaret Sanger (the founder of Planned Parenthood); and Winston Churchill. Indeed, as home secretary from 1910 to 1911, Churchill argued for eugenic government intervention regarding people categorized at the time as “feeble-minded” or “insane.” In addition, major early philanthropic foundations like the Carnegie Institution and the Rockefeller Foundation provided extensive financial grants to eugenics organizations, such as the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, under the direction of leaders and trustees who subscribed to the pseudoscience of the era. This extended to the universities as well. James Rowland Angell, who was president of Yale from 1921 t0 1937, and Charles William Eliot, who was president of Harvard from 1869 to 1909, were outspoken and virulent eugenics supporters. (Elliott served as a vice president to the first International Eugenics Congress held in London in 1912.) The court itself perhaps most prominently embraced this movement in Buck v. Bell. In upholding Virginia’s compulsory sterilization law, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. wrote for the majority that: In the wake of the Supreme Court’s ruling, 70,000 Americans were compulsorily sterilized, and 32 states ended up adopting compulsory sterilization statutes like Virginia’s. Nazi jurists and race hygienists studied U.S. sterilization statutes, such as California’s eugenics programs, as well as the Buck v. Bell decision. These laws inspired Adolf Hitler’s Nazi government to pass a German eugenics law in July 1933 entitled a “Law for the Prevention of Offspring with Hereditary Diseases” a few months after the Nazis came to power. Ultimately, 400,000 people were sterilized by the German law. The same racist ideology that led to these compulsory sterilizations in Hitler’s Nazi Germany undoubtedly helped fuel the ideas behind the Holocaust. Such ideas could not be in greater contrast to the Lockean principle that “All men are born free and equal.” That idea was thriving in the 1780’s when the Constitution was adopted; it was thriving during Reconstruction and in President Abraham Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address; but by 1912 it had effectively died out. The “born free and equal” idea only reemerged in 1948 as an Article I right in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights after the horrors of the Nazis and the Holocaust began coming to light. Buck v. Bell was egregiously wrong not only as a matter of morals, but under the “birthright equality” principle that underlies the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment. Citizens, as I explained in my prior articles, are born equal (i.e., they are born to be neither slaves nor lords). The citizenship clause grants equal rights unto the feeble-minded and the geniuses of this world alike. The right to have children, like the right to marry (the purpose of which is often to have children) is obviously deeply rooted in American history and tradition. The Preamble of our Constitution states that one of the six purposes of that document is: “To secure the Blessings of Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity”. It goes without saying, I think, that a government which is compulsorily sterilizing its citizens based on a social worker’s finding of feeblemindedness is not securing the “Blessings of Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity.” The landmark 1823 decision of Corfield v. Coryell, which I have previously said is the 14th Amendment’s version of the “born free and equal” clauses, stated that: As noted, Americans cannot “enjoy … life and liberty” or “pursue and obtain happiness and safety” if they face the risk of compulsorily sterilization. But can such laws then be justified under Coryell’s rational basis test (in bold), i.e., that such laws are “just” and are enacted for the “general good of the whole [people]?” Certainly not. A government that could compulsorily sterilize the feeble-minded would also be able to compulsorily sterilize any population that has fallen out of favor, whether Jewish or Black people, Native Americans, or Latinos. Nor, even if such a policy for the “feebleminded” was justified, could it be properly implemented (as was true in Buck’s very own case). The Supreme Court distinguished but did not overrule Buck v. Bell in 1942’s Skinner v. Oklahoma after it became terribly apparent what eugenics led to. Someday, the Supreme Court should formally overrule this terrible precedent. In the meantime, Harvard Law School should cancel its annual, prestigious “Oliver Wendell Holmes Lecture.” Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. title: Liverpool v Tottenham Hotspur: Team news - Liverpool FC
content:
Andoni Iraola will carefully assess his Liverpool squad to determine who is ready to start Tuesday night's Carabao Cup tie with Tottenham Hotspur. A busy period for the Reds continues with Premier League opposition arriving at Anfield in the third round of the League Cup. There will be at least one change from the side that began the draw against Fulham at the weekend, with Iraola confirming Giorgi Mamardashvili is set to be in goal. Discussing his selection plans, the Liverpool head coach told reporters on Monday: "I think it [the workload] has to affect, definitely, because it's the third game. It's the worst scenario – it's game, two days, game, two days, game. "In terms of the schedule, we haven't been lucky because it's true that after this one we have a little bit more [time] before we play Bournemouth. "Also we had a little bit more [time] between Ipswich and Atletico Madrid, and you notice if it's four or five days in comparison to two, three days. It's a massive difference but it is what it is. "I think after the international break also we have this period, I think, we are playing in nine, 10 days, four games or something like this. So, we have to get used to this." He continued: "You can decide and put the same players [in] every game. The problem is there is going to be a moment where they are going to be very tired and there is more risk of injury. But that's why we cannot say it doesn't work for anyone. "There are players who play every three days, they have no issues, they are very robust, they can accept it, their performances don't change too much. And there are other players where the risk is bigger, the performances are different. "And also we are in a process where I have to learn who is ready to play three or four games in a row every two or three days and who needs a rest so the performance level doesn't get affected. "I think I have it in my mind quite clear with some of them but with others it's new even for them because they haven't played as many games and we are learning." You have to accept cookies in order to view this content on our site. Mamardashvili is in line for his first appearance of the 2026-27 campaign and is a goalkeeper held in high regard by Iraola. Asked about Liverpool's options between the posts, Iraola replied: "I think there are little doubts with Ali [Becker]. He's proven, he's playing very well. "I also rate Giorgi very highly. I know him from his years also in Spain. I told him we tried to sign him for Bournemouth before I came here. "For me, he's a very good 'keeper and he's going to start tomorrow, yes." Joe Gomez is fit again following the muscle injury he sustained in pre-season. "I think he's going to be available for tomorrow and now it's a matter of deciding how much he can play and what is the best thing to do," Iraola said. Conor Bradley, Federico Chiesa, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni remain sidelined. For Tottenham, Sandro Tonali is absent due to a knock, and Dejan Kulusevski and Pedro Porro are also out. Forward Richarlison will not feature, but Destiny Udogie is available after he missed the goalless draw with Everton last Saturday. Head coach Roberto De Zerbi told reporters on Monday: "Kulusevski is not available. Pedro is still not available. Udogie, yes. "Richarlison, nothing has changed for the Carabao Cup or Premier League, the situation is the same. No [he won't be involved]." On his selection plans for the tie, De Zerbi said: "The team selection is not difficult because I am lucky to have these players. I am convinced of the qualities of the players. "I think Lucas Bergvall is not other players. Mathys Tel also. And then we have to analyse the other players, maybe the players that didn't play enough. "I am lucky because in central defence I have Jan Paul van Hecke and Micky van de Ven, top centre-backs, but also Ben Davies, Marcos Senesi, Tosin [Adarabioyo] are not less than Van Hecke and Van de Ven." De Zerbi said 'I don't know' regarding a potential senior debut for academy player Luca Williams-Barnett and added: "I would like to play with the same attitude as in the Premier League. The attitude and spirit the same. "Many players need to play. Maybe not 90 minutes but 30 minutes. It is a real game. It is important." Legendary former Liverpool left-back Andy Robertson could make his first appearance against the Reds since he signed for Tottenham in the summer. title: Diablo V Promises More Classes Than Any Previous Diablo Game, as Blizzard Brings Back Procedural Overworlds and Diablo II Runewords - Wccftech
content:
Blizzard's most surprising reveal at BlizzCon 2026 was undoubtedly the announcement of Diablo V, of which we had had no rumors prior to the Opening Ceremony. Even more interesting is the fact that Diablo V won't be about stopping the titular Lord of Terror, but about what happens after he's already taken Sanctuary. That premise had fans excited about this twist, and the ‘Forging the Next Era’ panel offered them plenty of details about the project due in Spring 2029. The panel featured Blizzard president Johanna Faries as the host, while Senior Game Director Joe Shely, Senior Production Director Tiffany Wat, Senior Art Director John Mueller, Narrative Director Jennifer Hepler, and Executive Producer Matt Zitterman spoke about the game. The team began by breaking down the Diablo player base after 30 years, looking for the clusters within it: players there for the story and dark fantasy atmosphere, players there to grind bosses and min-max builds, and everyone in between. The goal was for every feature to be anchored to the kind of Diablo player it was primarily for. From there, they looked hard at Diablo IV, what worked, how it had evolved in response to feedback, and where they wanted to try something genuinely new. That conversation led to the expansion-versus-sequel question, and the answer came down to fundamentals. A sequel lets them change what the game fundamentally is, which is extremely difficult on top of a title several years, expansions, and seasons deep. There was also the small matter of the franchise's big bad himself. As Zitterman put it, Mephisto and Lilith were epic characters with real depth in Diablo IV and its expansions, and Diablo deserves that and more. Narrative director Jennifer Hepler laid out the central premise: for 30 years, players have been scrambling to protect Sanctuary before Diablo could rise. In Diablo V, other heroes rose to stop him, and they failed. The players will be living in the aftermath of what they failed to prevent. When the game begins, seven years will have passed since Diablo conquered Sanctuary. He now rules from the throne of Westmarch, wielding humanity's people and souls as weapons in the Eternal Conflict, with the conquest intended as a stepping stone toward his ultimate goal of invading the Heavens. The Western Continent has become an outpost of Hell. Few humans remain who haven't bowed or joined the cults, and a terrifying handful of powerful humans have been corrupted and elevated into Dread Commanders, wielding power rivaling the dukes of Hell. Anyone who resists ends up in a soul cage or is dragged into the Terror Realm, Diablo's personal corner of Hell. The player character is the Heir to Westmarch, and the story begins when they discover they can enter the Terror Realm and survive. Hepler was also firm on one point: the team briefly explored making Diablo a morally grey figure, given Blizzard's track record with Sylvanas and Lilith, but kept arriving at the same conclusion. Diablo is Diablo. He isn't redeemable or misunderstood. The question isn't whether he has a point, but what happens now that he's won. However, just like with Lilith, the player character has a mysterious personal connection to Diablo, revealed over the course of the game, which makes them both a genuine threat to him and uniquely vulnerable to his influence. Here's the significant headline mechanical change: procedural generation is back in both dungeons and the overworld. Tiffany Wat explained that the Dread Commanders are actively reshaping the land, a process the team affectionately calls Terror Forming. Returning to a region visited before, players could find the landmarks, terrain, monsters and rewards to be all different. The knock-on effect is that the knowledge accumulated yesterday does not necessarily help the player today. Joe Shely's pitch to his own team is that players should never feel quite safe, which is easier to achieve when all the towns are gone. Art director John Mueller described three visual lenses the team works through. The past covers everything lost, a life-after-people vision of a desolate Sanctuary. The present is where evil has touched the world, where the Dread Commanders have burned through, leaving something strange behind. The future is what the player hero will be trying to prevent: Hell breaking through entirely. Each Dread Commander brings their own distinct visual theme to the land they've corrupted. With every settlement already destroyed in this post-apocalyptic version of Sanctuary, Blizzard needed a new answer to the question of where safety lives. The solution is the caravan. Rather than moving between towns, players bring a traveling band of wagons and followers with them. The caravan grows upon meeting other survivors, and its members become merchants, crafters and companions. Zitterman compared the feeling to the Rogue Encampment in the original Diablo: humanity eking out a corner of safety, gathered around a campfire as the last bastion against the dark. The design consequence is more interesting than it first appears. There are no ordinary civilians left in Sanctuary, which means no quest givers waiting by the roadside. All side content, therefore, comes from the caravan members, and every quest is part of the personal story of someone brought along. Two companions were teased. Blizzard confirmed a former Sister of the Sightless Eye, and the panel spent rather longer on a treasure goblin named Zarg, who is joining up simply because he understands that the player character is considerably easier to steal from than Diablo is. Joe Shely announced the first three classes that will be in Diablo V: The big claim is that Diablo V will launch with more classes than any previous Diablo game, and Joe specified he means more total classes, not just more at ship than a given entry had at its own launch. The game's itemization pillars are depth, clarity, and identity, and the whole approach is explicitly inspired by Diablo II. Items start simple and grow with the player. Large items once again occupy multiple inventory slots, which the art team is enjoying for the bigger icons and the familiarity. Controller players worried about manipulating a grid inventory were assured that the team has solutions in mind. Gear-based sets are returning, too. The team liked what the talisman did in the Lord of Hatred expansion for Diablo IV, but wanted to reattach the set concept to gear itself, because picking up one piece and recognizing it as part of a larger whole creates its own quest. They also say they have ideas for making sets broaden the range of viable builds rather than narrowing them. Blizzard's official write-up adds something the panel didn't state outright: the crafting system will be rich and deep, inspired by Lord of Hatred's approach, and will include Diablo II-style Runes and Runewords. Finally, the team is experimenting with stat requirements for items, though that isn't confirmed yet. Zitterman was upfront about why Blizzard is announcing a game that's still years out: they want community feedback as early as possible, and want players involved in the process rather than presented with a finished product. Regular updates are set to begin next year, with Blizzard already collecting sign-ups on the official website in the meantime. title: Norway bids final farewell to popular King Harald V as crowds and royals converge for his funeral - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
content: Norway has bid its final farewell to Harald V as crowds line the streets and foreign royals and leaders converge on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king OSLO, Norway -- Norway bade its final farewell to Harald V on Wednesday as crowds lined the streets and foreign royals and leaders converged on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king, who was remembered as a popular monarch with a down-to-earth touch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the capital at the start of a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald’s son, new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, draped with the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed in a car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the solemn procession. They included the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Also present were the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino, as well as political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As the funeral service began, Norway came to a halt for a minute of silence. Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. He modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who recently abdicated. His son immediately became king and last week took an oath of allegiance to Norway’s constitution in parliament. The parliament's speaker, Masud Gharahkhani, said at the service that “King Harald was close to the people” and recalled that “he wasn’t afraid to meet people in his rubber boots.” He remembered Harald saying in his 2008 New Year's address: “I wish we would stop using the term ‘the weakest in society.’ In reality, some of these people are among the strongest of us all.” “He lived up to his motto: He gave his all for Norway,” Gharahkhani said. Large crowds flocked to Oslo for the funeral, and thousands stood behind barriers on streets lined with national flags. The downtown area was closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police had instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. People tuned in across the country of about 5.6 million. Scores of churches, libraries, cultural centers and city halls made big screens available for the public to watch the funeral, public broadcaster NRK reported. The government said it wasn’t an official holiday, but schools and workplaces could individually opt to let students and employees watch. Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin in the chapel of the royal palace. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend. Over 46,000 people visited the chapel during the week it lay in state. “The love between the people and King Harald has not ended — quite the contrary,” said Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit, who led the funeral service, pointing to the tributes left outside the palace after his death. “The sea of flowers, along with the words and drawings that accompany them, speaks loudly and clearly of a heart so full that it overflows.” After the funeral, Harald's coffin was taken in a smaller procession to Akershus Fortress, where his predecessors are buried in the crypt of the palace chapel. Haakon followed with the two other Scandinavian monarchs, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark. Among those who attended the funeral was Mette-Marit’s eldest son and Haakon's stepson, Marius Borg Høiby, who has no royal title or duties. Høiby is appealing against a rape conviction after a trial earlier this year that cast a shadow over the royal family. Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. The Norwegian royal house has kinfolk in other European royal families. Harald and Haakon are related to both Britain’s King Charles III and Spain’s King Felipe VI: They’re all descendants of the U.K.'s Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 until her death in 1901. Today, the throne's role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world. Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jamey Keaten in Geneva and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland contributed to this report. But I've never fancied it. It's a weather thing. Hence not so many in the rest of the country, I'm sure, although university campuses probably often have them, e.g. I think I've seen one at Bath.
